title: bitwise operations, masks, and subset enumeration
concepts: Bitwise operations act independently on corresponding binary digits; AND, OR, XOR, and NOT have truth-table behavior that should be reasoned about at the bit level.
A bit mask encodes a small set using one bit per element, enabling constant-time membership tests and compact subset state when the universe fits the integer width.
Setting, clearing, toggling, and testing a bit use masks built from a one shifted to the target position; shift counts and signed integer behavior are language-specific hazards.
XOR is self-inverse, so equal values cancel in pairs and x XOR 0 equals x; these identities support parity and unique-element techniques under precise multiplicity assumptions.
The expression x AND -x isolates the least significant set bit in two's-complement integer arithmetic; clearing it with x AND (x-1) supports population-count loops.
Enumerating all subsets takes O(2^n) masks; enumerating all submasks across every mask takes O(3^n) total pairs, which is useful only for small n.
Bit tricks can reduce constants or encode state compactly, but they do not remove exponential complexity when all subsets must be considered.
Fixed-width overflow, negative values, sign extension, and shifting by the type width can invalidate informal identities; state the integer representation and constraints.
